anchor: the deck known as the upper gun deck
note: A seventy-four had guns on two covered decks. The upper gun deck lay under the open spar-deck.

anchor: berth-deck, the latter
note: The berth-deck was the deck below the gun decks, where the crew’s bags were stowed.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Berth-deck”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: movable pantries of the many messes of the men
note: Each mess had a chest holding its food and dishes.

anchor: lying prone in irons
note: Prone: lying face down. In irons: fastened with shackles.

anchor: of the heavier calibre of that period
note: Calibre: the width of a gun’s bore, which sets the weight of its shot.

anchor: cumbersome harness of breechen and strong side-tackles
note: Breechings were thick ropes that held a gun back as it recoiled. Tackles were pulleys for running it out.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Breeching”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: the long rammers and shorter lintstocks
note: A rammer pushes the charge into a gun. A lintstock is a forked stick that holds the match.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Rammer”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: wore the like livery of the undertakers
note: Livery: a uniform. The black ropes look like undertakers’ black clothing.

anchor: white jumper and white duck trousers
note: A jumper was a loose sailor’s jacket. Duck is a heavy cotton or linen fabric.

anchor: like a patch of discolored snow in early April lingering at some upland cave’s black mouth
note: Melville compares Billy’s white clothes in the dark bay to snow left in a cave in spring.

anchor: two battle-lanterns swing from two massive beams
note: Battle-lanterns were heavy lanterns lit during action below decks.

anchor: the war-contractors
note: War-contractors supplied goods to the navy at a profit, and Melville sneers at them.

anchor: the tompioned cannon protrude
note: A tompion is a plug that keeps water and dust out of a gun’s muzzle.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Tompion”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: like small confessionals or side-chapels in a cathedral
note: Confessionals are booths where priests hear confession. Side-chapels are small chapels along a cathedral aisle.

anchor: no pallor could have shown
note: Pallor: paleness. His rosy tan would still hide any pallor.

anchor: days of sequestration
note: Sequestration: being shut away from light and air.

anchor: as nipped in the vice of fate
note: Nipped: caught tight and held. Vice: a tool that grips.

anchor: the diabolical incarnate
note: Incarnate: embodied in flesh. Billy has met evil in a person.

anchor: the gyved one’s trance
note: Gyved: shackled with gyves, old word for fetters.

anchor: a serene happy light born of some wandering reminiscence
note: Reminiscence: a memory, here a happy dream of the past.

anchor: peradventure feeling
note: Peradventure: perhaps, maybe, as the chaplain might think.

anchor: tho’ receiving his stipend from Mars
note: Mars was the Roman god of war. The chaplain is paid by the war department.

anchor: but it was something in the way that children will refer to death in general
note: Billy talks of death without fear, as children play at funerals.

anchor: those so-called barbarous ones
note: Barbarous: uncivilized, in the language of Melville’s time.

anchor: the British captives, living trophies, made to march in the Roman triumph of Germanicus
note: Germanicus was a Roman general who celebrated a triumph in Rome on 26 May, A.D. 17, after his German campaigns.

anchor: Fra Angelico’s seraphs
note: Fra Angelico was an Italian painter of the 1400s, famous for his serene, gentle angels.

anchor: gardens of the Hesperides
note: In Greek myth the Hesperides were the maidens who guarded a garden of golden apples.

anchor: the skull, dial, and cross-bones on old tombstones
note: Old gravestones carried a skull, an hourglass or dial, and crossed bones as reminders of death.

anchor: superior savage so called
note: Melville uses the word “savage” in the manner of his time.

anchor: a Tahitian say of Captain Cook’s time
note: Captain James Cook visited Tahiti on voyages in the late 1700s, and missionaries followed soon after.

anchor: a felon in martial law
note: Felon: a person guilty of a serious crime.

anchor: the confines of death
note: Confines: borders, limits, the edge between life and death.

anchor: an irruption of heretic thought
note: Irruption: a sudden entering. Heretic: contrary to accepted belief.

anchor: a martyr to martial discipline
note: A martyr suffers or dies for a cause.

anchor: the minister of the Prince of Peace serving in the host of the God of War
note: Isaiah calls the coming Messiah the Prince of Peace. Mars is the Roman war god. The chaplain serves both.
source: The Bible (King James Version), Isaiah 9:6, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

anchor: he indirectly subserves the purpose attested by the cannon
note: Subserves: serves as a means to.

anchor: the abrogation of everything but brute Force
note: Abrogation: the abolishing of a law or custom.
